steps.body: The full pipeline: **pose a statistical question → decide who to ask → collect one value per person → look for the pattern.** Every later tool in this course (plots, averages, spreads) works on data born this way. A weak question — or mixed-up collection — poisons everything downstream, so the pipeline's first step matters most.
Design the sampling step of a statistical investigation and separate bias from variability.

widget.prompt: You want to describe all students in the school. Build a representative sample and run it several times.
widget.successFeedback: Stratifying across grade groups reduces selection bias; a larger sample reduces random variability.
widget.methodFeedback: Asking only the easiest students to reach can stay biased even with many responses.
widget.sizeFeedback: The selection is representative, but a larger sample will reduce random variability.
widget.drawsFeedback: Repeat the sample so you can see variability instead of trusting one result.

predict.prompt: In a data investigation, what must exist BEFORE any data gets collected?

options.label: Nothing — collect the data first, decide the question after

predict.reveal: Data is an answer — without a question first, there's nothing to collect and no way to know what counts. Collect first and decide later, and you end up with a pile of numbers gathered by no rule — no way to tell which values matter or what they settle. The question steers everything after it.

cml.actionGoal: Build a representative design and distinguish bias from random variation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Make the sample ten times larger without changing a biased method. Which problem remains?

explanation.prompt: Why can a very large convenience sample still be misleading?

options.label: It can repeatedly overrepresent the same easy-to-reach group.
options.feedback: Exactly — size cannot repair a biased selection process.

options.label: Large samples are always accurate.
options.feedback: Large samples can be precisely wrong when selection is biased.

explanationVariants: "How tall is the flagpole?" has one answer — the pipeline fails at step one because the question isn't statistical.
No variability is anticipated, so there's no distribution to collect or study.

widget.prompt: A student plans a survey around "How tall is the school flagpole?" Where does the pipeline break?

options.label: Step one — the question isn't statistical (one fixed answer)
options.feedback: Right — one flagpole, one height. There's no variability to study, so no survey can fix it.

options.label: Step three — measuring flagpoles is too hard
options.feedback: Difficulty isn't the issue; even measured perfectly, there's only ONE value. The question itself anticipates no variability.

options.label: Nothing breaks — any question works
options.feedback: A data pipeline needs anticipated variability from step one. A single fixed answer gives nothing to distribute or summarize.

hints: Check the question against the ch1 test.
One flagpole, one height — not statistical.

steps.body: A well-run pipeline still produces MESSY-looking data — that's normal and good. "How many pets?" giving 0,1,1,2,2,2,3,4 isn't a mistake; the spread IS the finding. Variability isn't noise to eliminate — it's the signal the statistical question set out to capture.

explanationVariants: Differing answers are exactly what a statistical question anticipates — the spread is the finding, not a flaw.
If every answer matched, the question would have been non-statistical to begin with.

widget.prompt: A survey's answers are all different from each other. Did something go wrong?

options.label: No — variability is exactly what the statistical question anticipated
options.feedback: Right — the differences are the phenomenon under study, not a collection error.

options.label: Yes — good data should agree
options.feedback: That's backwards for statistical questions: identical answers would mean no variability, i.e. nothing statistical to study.

options.label: Yes — the survey should be rerun until answers match
options.feedback: Rerunning to force agreement would erase the signal. The spread of answers IS the finding.

hints: What did the statistical question anticipate?

widget.prompt: You ask all 30 students in the gym "how many jumping jacks can you do in a minute?" — but 2 students decline to answer. How many values does your data set end up with?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 counts everyone ASKED, but a value only exists when someone ANSWERS: 30 − 2 = 28.
2 is the number who declined. The data holds the answers you DID get: 30 − 2 = 28.

explanationVariants: "Minutes spent reading last night" fixes what's measured and who's asked; "do students read a lot?" is too vague to collect one clean value per person.
A collectible question specifies the measurement; a vague one can't produce comparable values.

widget.prompt: Which version is READY for data collection?

options.label: Minutes each student read last night
options.feedback: Right — one clear number per student, all measuring the same thing.

options.label: Whether students read a lot
options.feedback: "A lot" isn't measurable — each person would interpret it differently, so the values wouldn't be comparable.

options.label: Whether reading is beneficial
options.feedback: An opinion prompt with no measurement at all — nothing numeric to collect per person.

hints: Which produces one comparable number per person?
Vague words like "a lot" can't be measured.

steps.body: Complete the pipeline by drawing one value for every team member.
hints: The question asks every player for one count: goals scored this season.
Use the recorded frequencies to build the stacks.
The five stack heights must add to 12 players.
explanationVariants: The stack heights 1, 3, 4, 2, and 2 add to 12, so every player contributes exactly one goal-count value.
The finished plot connects the statistical question, the 12 observed values, and the pattern in their variation.

widget.prompt: All 12 players answered, 'How many goals did you score this season?' Build the data: 1 player scored 0, 3 scored 1, 4 scored 2, 2 scored 3, and 2 scored 4.
widget.successFeedback: The plot contains 1 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 12 dots — one observed value per player. Now the spread is visible as the final pattern in the question-to-data pipeline.
widget.partialFeedback: Some stacks do not match the recorded responses. Recount each goal value; the finished plot must contain exactly 12 dots.

steps.body: The pipeline, sound at every joint.
takeaways: Question → who to ask → one value per answer → pattern.
Variability in the data is the finding, not an error.
A collectible question names a concrete measurement; values come only from answers received.
steps.teaser: next chapter: SEEING the data — dot plots and histograms.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **The pipeline starts with a statistical question and ends with a pattern.** Ask a group a measurable question, record one value per answer, and the spread you see is the finding.

explanationVariants: The question comes first — everything downstream depends on it anticipating variability.
No statistical question, no meaningful data.

widget.prompt: What is the FIRST step of the data pipeline?

options.label: Pose a statistical question
options.feedback: Right — the question defines what's measured and anticipates the variability everything else studies.

options.label: Collect values
options.feedback: Collection needs a question to collect answers TO. The question comes first.

options.label: Look for a pattern
options.feedback: The pattern is the LAST step — it needs collected values, which need a question first.
